rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is not enough to refute those who require the blessing by noting that no Companion or Successor report against obligation was preserved; one would need an explicit transmitted consensus of non-obligation.
rows.anchor: فكيف يسعهم خرق الإجماع على أنه لا يكفي في الرد عليهم كونه لم يحفظ عن صحابي أو تابعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that performing the blessing leaves no time for other worship is denied: one can devote time to other acts of worship.
rows.anchor: وأما الثاني فممنوع بل يمكن التفرغ لعبادات أخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proponents of obligation can accept the third objection's consequence; the author says it entails no hardship.
rows.anchor: فللقائلين بالوجوب إلتزامه وليس فيه حرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars explicitly state that the obligation also applies with respect to God, answering the fourth objection.
rows.anchor: فلأن جمعا صرحوا بالوجوب في حقه تعالى أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several routes from Companions report that when they addressed the Prophet, they said, May God bless you.
rows.anchor: ورد في عدة طرق عن عدة من الصحابة أنهم لما قالوا : يارسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sixth objection cannot be answered by interpreting the hadiths as proposed without supplying the supporting chain of evidence.
rows.anchor: حمل الأحاديث على ما ذكر لا يكفي إلا مع بيان سنده ولم يبينوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those requiring the blessing differ: most make it an individual duty for every person, while some regard it as a communal duty.
rows.anchor: أكثرهم على أن ذلك فرض عين على كل فرد فرد وبعضهم على أنه فرض كفاية

rows.speaker: صاحب المجتبى
rows.claim: Whether the duty recurs with every mention of the Prophet in one gathering is disputed: one commentary says once suffices as the sound view, while the Mujtaba says it recurs.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض شروح الهداية يكفي مرة على الصحيح وقال صاحب المجتبي : يتكرر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing is not repeated with each mention of God; a proposed distinction is that divine rights allow leniency while human rights are strict, but calling this God's right merely because He commanded it misunderstands the intended category.
rows.anchor: وفي تكرر ذكر الله تعالى لا يتكرر وفرق هو وغيره بينهما بما فيه نظر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i's established position requires the blessing in the final sitting of prayer, between tashahhud and the concluding salutation; al-Asnawi transmits another view calling it a sunna, which leading Shafi'i scholars did not adopt.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنها تجب في القعود آخر الصلاة بين التشهد وسلام التحلل وهذا هو مذهب الشافعي

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud authentically said that after tashahhud in prayer, a person blesses the Prophet and then makes personal supplication.
rows.anchor: فقد صح عنه أنه قال : يتشهد الرجل في الصلاة ثم يصلي

rows.speaker: أبو مسعود البدري وابن عمر
rows.claim: Abu Masud al-Badri and Ibn Umar authentically say a prayer includes recitation, tashahhud, and blessing on the Prophet; omission of any calls for two prostrations after the salutation.
rows.anchor: فقد صح عنهما أنه لا تكون صلاة إلا بقراءة وتشهد وصلاة على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi says they taught tashahhud, then praise and glorification of God, blessing on the Prophet, and finally asking one's need.
rows.anchor: الشعبي فقد صح عنه كنا نعلم التشهد فإذا قال : وأن محمدا عبده ورسوله

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits from al-Shaʿbi that one who omits blessing on the Prophet in tashahhud must repeat the prayer, or else that the prayer does not suffice.
rows.anchor: وأخرج البيهقي عنه من لم يصل على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في التشهد فليعد صلاته

rows.speaker: محمد الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi relates a similar view from Muhammad al-Baqir, which al-Daraqutni judged sound.
rows.anchor: والإمام أبو جعفر محمد الباقر فقد روى البيهقي عنه نحو ما ذكر عن الشعبي وصوبه الدارقطني

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar says he found no Companion or Successor explicitly denying obligation except Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, suggesting the others held it obligatory.
rows.anchor: لم أر عن أحد من الصحابة والتابعين التصريح بعدم الوجوب إلا ما نقل عن إبراهيم النخعي

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: Ahmad has two transmitted positions, and the author considers the later report to be obligation: Ahmad said he had hesitated but then concluded the blessing was obligatory.
rows.anchor: فإنه قال : كنت أتهيب ذلك ثم تبينت فإذا الصلاة على النبي

rows.speaker: إسحاق بن راهويه
rows.claim: In Ishaq ibn Rahwayh's later report, deliberately omitting the blessing invalidates prayer, while for forgetful omission he hopes the prayer suffices; this is also a Malikite position chosen by Ibn al-Arabi.
rows.anchor: إذا تركها عمدا بطلت صلاته أو سهوا رجوت أن تجزئة وهو قول عند المالكية أختاره إبن العربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Requiring blessing at every mention would entail it in tashahhud, but requiring it there does not make it a condition of prayer's validity; this evidence rebuts the claim that al-Shafiʿi innovated by requiring it.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه يرد على القائلين بأن الشافعي رضي الله تعالى عنه شذ في قوله بالوجوب

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi's argument is set out in al-Umm; his followers defend it with hadiths of differing strength and wrote treatises answering critics including Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Khattabi, and al-Tahawi.
rows.anchor: وأما دليله رضي الله تعالى عنه على ذلك فمذكور في الأم وقد استدل له أصحابه بعدة أحاديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author condemns attacking an imam like al-Shafiʿi and calls partisanship without adequate investigation reprehensible; the discussion of salutation follows the same debate as that of blessing.
rows.anchor: وأنا أرى التشنيع على مثل هذا الإمام شنيعا والتعصب مع قلة التتبع أمرا فظيعا

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris says blessing and salutation share the same obligatory status because both are commanded in the verse, and a command denotes obligation unless evidence redirects it.
rows.anchor: صرح ابن فارس اللغوي بأنهما سيان في الفرضية لأن كلا منهما مأمور به في الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best formula is the one the Prophet taught his Companions when they asked, since he would choose the finest form for himself.
rows.anchor: وأفضل الكيفيات في الصلاة عليه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم ما علمه رسول الله عليه الصلاة والسلام لأصحابه

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawi says in al-Rawda that someone who vows to bless the Prophet in the best manner fulfills the vow only with the Prophetic formula taught to the Companions.
rows.anchor: قال النووي في الروضة : لو حلف ليصلين على النبي

rows.speaker: السبكي
rows.claim: Al-Subki explains that this formula certainly performs the requested blessing and brings the reward mentioned in hadiths for that form.
rows.anchor: ووجهه السبكي بأن من أتى بها فقد صلى الصلاة المطلوبة بيقين وكان له الخير الوارد في أحاديث الصلاة كذلك

rows.speaker: المروزي
rows.claim: Al-Marwazi holds that a person fulfills the vow with the formula asking blessings on Muhammad and his family whenever those who remember remember and those who forget overlook.
rows.anchor: ونقل الرافعي عن المروزي أنه يبر باللهم صل على محمد وآل محمد كلما ذكرك الذاكرون

rows.speaker: القاضي حسين
rows.claim: Qadi Husayn's proposed vow-fulfilling formula is, O God, bless Muhammad as befits and is due to him.
rows.anchor: وقال القاضي حسين : طريق البر اللهم صل على محمد كما هو أهله ومستحقه

rows.speaker: البارزي
rows.claim: Al-Barizi prefers a formula asking God for the best blessings on Muhammad and his family, in a number equal to God's known things.
rows.anchor: واختار البارزي أن الأفضل اللهم صل على محمد وعلى آل محمد أفضل صلواتك وعدد معلوماتك

rows.speaker: الكمال بن الهمام
rows.claim: Kamal ibn al-Humam says all mentioned formulas are contained in an expansive prayer asking God's finest blessings, honor, and nearness for the Prophet and his family.
rows.anchor: وقال الكمال بن الهمام : كلما ذكر من الكيفيات موجود في اللهم صل أبدا أفضل صلواتك

rows.speaker: ابن حجر الهيثمي
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar al-Haytami selects yet another formula as the best, without its wording being specified here.
rows.anchor: واختار ابن حجر الهيثمي غير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عبد السلام
rows.claim: Ibn Abd al-Salam, as transmitted by Ibn Arafa, requires an added taslīm in the salutation wording; al-Alusi says that appeal to the verse's surface wording is unsound on reflection.
rows.anchor: ونقل ابن عرفة عن ابن عبدالسلام أنه لا بد في السلام عليه صل الله تعالى عليه وسلم أن يزيد تسليما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group of Companions and later authorities held that blessing is not confined to transmitted formulas if an eloquent wording clearly expresses the Prophet's honor and high status.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن جمع من الصحابة ومن بعدهم أن كيفية الصلاة عليه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لا يوقف فيها مع المنصوص

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud advises making the blessing beautiful because it may be presented to the Prophet; when asked for wording, he gives a long invocation for blessings, mercy, and the Prophet's praiseworthy station, ending with the Abrahamic formula.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود رضي الله تعالى عنه قال : إذا صليتم على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فأحسنوا الصلاة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording subtly signals that blessing should be rendered beautifully: the phrase can form a hemistich of the kāmil meter, a subtle point the author regards as valuable.
rows.anchor: رمز خفي فيما أرى إلى مطلوبية تحسين الصلاة عليه عليه الصلاة والسلام حيث أتى به كلاما يصلح أن يكون شطرا من البحر الكامل

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawi and some others infer that separating blessing from salutation is disliked because the verse commands both together; critics cite teaching reports in which salutation came first, but the response is that the order was incidental, not deliberate separation.
rows.anchor: واستدل النووي رحمه الله تعالى بالآية على كراهة إفراد الصلاة عن السلام وعكسه لورود الأمر بهما معا فيها

rows.speaker: ابن حجر الهيثمي
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar al-Haytami says the intended dislike is only خلاف الأولى, since no specific evidence establishing the cause for a stronger prohibition exists.
rows.anchor: وذكر العلامة ابن حجر الهيثمي أن الحق أن المراد بالكراهة خلاف الأولى إذ لم يوجد مقتضيها من النهي المخصوص

rows.speaker: الحموي
rows.claim: Al-Hamawi transmits from Minyat al-Mufti that Hanafis do not consider separating either blessing or salutation disliked; Mirak says this disagreement concerns the Prophet, while other prophets may be addressed separately without dislike.
rows.anchor: ونقل الحموي من أصحابنا عن منية المفتي أنه لا يكره عندنا أفراد أحدهما عن الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some restrict the dislike to separating the phrases in speech, not in writing, as occurs in al-Umm.
rows.anchor: وصرح بعضهم أن الكراهة عند من يقول بها إنما هي في الأفراد لفظا وأما الأفراد خطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds the verse a very weak proof for disliking separation: it commands blessing and salutation absolutely, without requiring them at the same time; one could bless in the morning and salute in the evening and fulfill the commands.
rows.anchor: إذ قصارى ما تدل عليه أن كلا من الصلاة والتسليم مأمور به مطلقا ولا تدل على الأمر بالإتيان بهما في زمان واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse does not require simultaneous pairing, most early Muslims combined the two; the author dislikes abandoning that practice, which also avoids an unlikely irreverent misunderstanding.
rows.anchor: نعم درج أكثر السلف على الجمع بينهما فلا أستحسن العدول عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars disagree whether the Prophet himself is included in the address to believers; some include him, and leading Shafiʿis expressly require him to bless himself even in prayer.
rows.anchor: وفي دخوله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم في الخطاب بيا أيها الذين آمنوا هنا خلاف فقال بعضهم بالدخول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports show the Prophet blessing and saluting himself outside prayer, including when a hypocrite rejoiced that his camel was lost and when he discussed returning property taken from his son-in-law Abu al-As before the latter's conversion; narrator insertion is very unlikely.
rows.anchor: كان يصلي على نفسه خارجها كما هو ظاهر أحاديث كقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم حين ضلت ناقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exclude the Prophet from the address because its surrounding context runs from the command not to enter the Prophet's houses to this command; the author replies that the earlier command is explicitly restricted to believers, while this verse has no such restriction.
rows.anchor: لا تدخلوا بيوت النبي ) إلى هنا ظاهرة في اختصاص هذا الحكم بالمؤمنين دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Usul scholars variously exclude the Prophet from such an address (a weak view), include him absolutely (called sound by a group), or include him except in commands to convey; the author includes him unless a contextual indicator excludes him, and finds such indicators here.
rows.anchor: وهو شاذ ودخوله مطلقا وهو الأصح على ما قال جمع والدخول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using believers rather than all people may signal that blessing the Prophet is a supreme and beneficial means unavailable to unbelievers; more likely, it both fits the context and urges believers to comply.
rows.anchor: وعبر بالذين آمنوا دون الناس الشامل للكفار قيل : إشارة إلى أن الصلاة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to bless and salute the Prophet is a distinctive privilege of this community; no other community was commanded to bless and salute its prophet.
rows.anchor: والأمر بالصلاة والتسليم من خواص هذه الأمة فلم تؤمر أمة غيرها بالصلاة والتسليم على نبيها

rows.speaker: أبو ذر الهروي
rows.claim: Abu Dharr al-Harawi reports that the command came in the second year after the Hijra; another view places it on the Night Journey, which the author regards as inconsistent with the verse's Medinan status.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك على ما نقل عن أبي ذر الهروي في السنة الثانية من الهجرة وقيل : كان في ليلة الإسراء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reports that when the verse was revealed Abu Bakr said every good thing sent to the Prophet was shared with them, after which the verse saying God and His angels bless the believers was revealed; the author says the differing styles have an evident wisdom.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر عن مجاهد أنها لما نزلت قال أبو بكر : ما أنزل الله عليك خيرا إلا أشركنا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blessing other prophets is permitted without dislike; a sound report, according to al-Majd al-Lughawi, tells people to include the Prophet when blessing the messengers, with another route judged good but mursal.
rows.anchor: والصلاة منا على الأنبياء ما عدا نبينا عليه وعليهم الصلاة والسلام جائزة بلا كراهة

rows.speaker: المجد اللغوي
rows.claim: The report also gives a wording: when people salute the Prophet, they should salute the messengers as well; the blessing wording has an additional good but mursal route.
rows.anchor: وفي لفظ إذا سلمتم علي فسلموا على المرسلين وللأول طريق أخرى إسنادها حسن جيد لكنه مرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No text is known specifically for blessing angels; the practice is inferred from Abu Hurayra's report if it is established that God called angels messengers.
rows.anchor: لصلاة على الملائكة قيل لا يعرف فيها نص وإنما تؤخذ من حديث أبي هريرة المذكور آنفا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet's instruction to bless God's prophets and messengers, whom God sent as He sent him; al-Alusi says its weak routes can be acted upon in this kind of matter.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : صلوا على أنبياء الله ورسله

rows.speaker: القاضي عياض
rows.claim: On blessing people other than prophets and angels, Qadi Iyad says it is absolutely permitted, as do most scholars; he cites 33:43 and Prophetic prayers for families and individuals, including a woman and her husband.
rows.anchor: فقيل تجوز مطلقا قال القاضي عياض وعليه عامة أهل العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evidence for general permission includes the Prophet's prayers for the family of Abu Awfa and the family of Saʿd ibn Ubada, and Ibn Hibban's sound report of a woman asking him to bless her and her husband.
rows.anchor: وبما صح من قوله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم اللهم صل على آل أبي أوفى

rows.speaker: مسلم
rows.claim: A report in Muslim says angels tell the believer's soul, May God bless you and your body; this counters al-Khafaji's claim that angels bless the community only through following the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وفي خبر مسلم أن الملائكة تقول لروح المؤمن : صلى الله عليك وعلى جسدك

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Another view, chosen by al-Qurtubi and others, forbids blessing anyone independently but permits it in a textually established dependent form, such as for the Prophet's family, or by analogy for Companions.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا تجوز استقلالا وتجوز تبعا فيما ورد فيه النص كالآل أو الحق به كالأصحاب وأختاره القرطبي

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: A view attributed to Abu Hanifa and a group allows blessing others only dependently, never independently.
rows.anchor: وقيل تجوز تبعا مطلقا ولا تجوز استقلالا ونسب إلى أبي حنيفة وجمع

rows.speaker: البيري
rows.claim: The Hanafi text Tanwir al-Absar bars blessing anyone besides prophets and angels except dependently; al-Bayri says the ruling is sinful and disliked, and this is the sound position, while the exact degree of dislike is otherwise open to interpretation.
rows.anchor: وفي تنوير الأبصار ولا يصلي على غير الأنبياء والملائكة إلا بطريق التبع

rows.speaker: الشافعية
rows.claim: A report from Ahmad regards independent blessing as disliked; the Shafiʿi position calls it خلاف الأولى.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية عن أحمد كراهة ذلك استقلالا ومذهب الشافعية أنه خلاف الأولى

rows.speaker: القاضي عياض
rows.claim: Al-Laqqani transmits Qadi Iyad's preference for restricting blessing and salutation to the Prophet and other prophets, with others instead mentioned through requests for forgiveness and approval as in 59:10; its use is said to have begun among early generations as a Rafidite innovation for some imams.
rows.anchor: أنه يجب تخصيص النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم وسائر الأنبياء بالصلاة والتسليم كما يختص الله سبحانه عند ذكره بالتقديس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi accepts that imitating innovators is disliked when the imitated act is blameworthy and the imitation is intended, but rejects a blanket application of that rule.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أن كراهة التشبه بأهل البدع مقررة عندنا أيضا لكن لا مطلقا بل في المذموم وفيما قصد به التشبه بهم

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: With a good or sound chain, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz wrote to his governor that storytellers had newly extended the Prophet's blessing to their allies and clients; he ordered prayer for prophets alone and general supplication for Muslims.
rows.anchor: وجاء عن عمر بن عبدالعزيز بسند حسن أو صحيح أنه كتب لعامله إن ناسا من القصاص قد أحدثوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas authentically says that no one should bless anyone except the Prophet; another version says to seek forgiveness for Muslim men and women instead. Both reports could indicate either dislike or prohibition.
rows.anchor: وصح عن ابن عباس أنه قال : لا تنبغي الصلاة من أحد على أحد إلا على النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who prohibit independent blessing argue that it became a distinctive honorific for prophets, just as عز وجل became a distinctive expression for God despite others being honored; they answer that God and His Messenger may grant such wording to whomever they choose, unlike others absent their permission.
rows.anchor: واستدل المانعون بأن لفظ الصلاة صار شعارا لعظم الأنبياء وتوقيرهم فلا تقال لغيرهم استقلالا

rows.speaker: أبو اليمن بن عساكر
rows.claim: Abu al-Yumn ibn Asakir says the Prophet may bless anyone because it is his prerogative and office, whereas the community may not bestow on another what belongs to him; the Shafiʿi Muʿtamad disputes that special privilege for lack of proof.
rows.anchor: ومن ثم قال أبو اليمن بن عساكر له صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم أن يصلي على غيره مطلقا لأنه حقه ومنصبه

rows.speaker: البيهقي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi reconciles prohibition when blessing serves as an honorific greeting and permission when it is a prayer or request for blessing.
rows.anchor: وحمل البيهقي بالمنع على ما إذا جعل ذلك تعظيما وتحية وبالجواز عليها إذا كان دعاء وتبركا

rows.speaker: بعض الحنابلة
rows.claim: Some Hanbalis allow independent blessing for the Prophet's family and general blessing for angels and the devout, but dislike or possibly forbid it for a named person or group, especially as an exclusive slogan for someone not equal or superior to the Prophet; occasional instances are allowed by Prophetic precedent.
rows.anchor: واختار بعض الحنابلة أن الصلاة على الآل مشروعة تبعا وجائزة استقلالا وعلى الملائكة وأهل الطاعة عموما جائزة أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the evidence can be reconciled without that particular Hanbali distinction; many apply the same rules to salutation as to blessing.
rows.anchor: وبهذا التفصيل تتفق الأدلة وأنت تعلم اتفاقها بغير ما ذكر والسلام عند كثير فيما ذكر

rows.speaker: الجويني
rows.claim: Al-Juwayni, as quoted by al-Laqqani, treats salutation like blessing: it is not used of an absent person or independently for a non-prophet, so say Ali, may God be pleased with him, rather than peace be upon him; the author questions the claim of consensus, while direct greetings to those present are permitted.
rows.anchor: أنه في معنى الصلاة فلا يستعمل في الغائب ولا يفرد به غير الأنبياء عليهم السلام فلا يقال علي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الدر المنضود
rows.claim: Al-Durr al-Mandud treats salutation like blessing, except for a present person or as a greeting to a living person who is absent.
rows.anchor: وفي الدر المنضود السلام كالصلاة فيما ذكر إلا إذا كان لحاضر أو تحية لحي غائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some distinguish salutation from blessing because it applies to every believer; the author calls this distinction circular and unsupported, and says the liturgical phrase peace upon us and God's righteous servants is a specific, dependent case.
rows.anchor: وفرق آخرون بأنه يشرع في حق كل مؤمن بخلاف الصلاة وهو فرق بالمدعي فلا يقبل

rows.speaker: التقي السبكي
rows.claim: A refined distinction, attributed to Taqi al-Subki, allows ordinary greeting to the living or dead at meetings or grave visits, with a response required of the present person or conveyed for the absent; salutation as a prayer that God grant peace is reserved for the Prophet except dependently.
rows.anchor: الذي يعم الحي والميت هو الذي يقصد به التحية كالسلام عند تلاق أو زيارة قبر

rows.speaker: الحليمي
rows.claim: The prayer-like salutation is what al-Halimi says is meant when he describes blessing as having the meaning of salutation; it requests that God confer peace and therefore carries a form of exaltation.
rows.anchor: وهذا النوع من السلام هو الذي ادعى الحليمي كون الصلاة بمعناه

rows.speaker: ابن عبد البر
rows.claim: Ibn Abd al-Barr forbids asking mercy for the Prophet; al-Alusi replies that sound hadiths attest it, including the tashahhud greeting with mercy and blessing, a Bedouin's prayer for himself and Muhammad that the Prophet approved, and other invocations.
rows.anchor: واختلف في جواز الدعاء له صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بالرحمة فذهب ابن عبدالبر إلى منع ذلك ورد بوروده في الأحاديث الصحيحة

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: A view taken by al-Suyuti and others, reported from the majority by Qadi Iyad and called correct by al-Qurtubi, permits asking mercy only when joined to blessing or salutation; al-Ghazali likewise forbids an unaccompanied request.
rows.anchor: وقد أخذ به جمع منهم الجلال السيوطي بل نقله القاضي عياض في الإكمال عن الجمهور

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali cites 24:63 and argues that, although blessing can mean mercy, prophets are distinguished by the honorific blessing, which for them is more specific than ordinary mercy.
rows.anchor: ويدل له قوله تعالى ( لا تجعلوا دعاء الرسول بينكم كدعاء بعضكم بعضا )

rows.speaker: ابن حجر الهيثمي
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar al-Haytami says the Bedouin's prayer for mercy, approved by the Prophet, shows that mercy may be requested without accompanying blessing or salutation; this specific approval takes precedence over the verse's general implication.
rows.anchor: قال ابن حجر الهيثمي : وهو الذي يتجه وتقريره المذكور خاص فيقدم على العموم الذي اقتضته الآية

rows.speaker: ابن حجر الهيثمي
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar interprets those who say such a request is impermissible as denying neutral permissibility, allowing that it is disliked or خلاف الأولى; Zayn al-Din says they agree one should not initiate the formula may God have mercy on him, a recommendation al-Alusi endorses.
rows.anchor: وينبغي حمل قول من قال لا يجوز ذلك على أن مرادهم نفي الجواز المستوي الطرفين

rows.speaker: الطحطاوي
rows.claim: Al-Tahtawi advises against saying may God forgive or pardon the Prophet because it may imply a deficiency; al-Alusi leans the same way, while noting that seeking forgiveness need not imply sin and can request higher rank, as the Prophet sought forgiveness repeatedly.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن لا يجوز غفر الله تعالى له أو سامحه لما فيه من إيهام النقص وهو الذي أميل إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author's preferred caution against asking forgiveness or pardon does not mean such prayer entails a sin; the Quran's wording is God's prerogative, and mercy for angels should be treated like mercy for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وأرى حكم الترحم على الملائكة عليهم السلام كحكم الترحم عليه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a person whose prophethood is disputed, such as Luqman, say may God be pleased with him, or include him in a prayer on the prophets, rather than independently assigning him the Prophet's formula.
rows.anchor: ومن اختلف في نبوته كلقمان يقال فيه رضي الله تعالى عنه أو صلى الله تعالى على الأنبياء وعليه وسلم

words: قُلْ مَن يَرْزُقُكُم مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is ordered to ask who provides from heaven and earth to corner the polytheists into admitting their idols own nothing, while God alone provides; they do not actually deny this.
rows.anchor: أمر صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يقول ذلك تبكيتا للمشركين بحملهم على الإقرار بأن آلهتهم لا يملكون مثقال ذرة في السموات ولا في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the opponents sometimes faltered to avoid the implication, the Prophet is told to answer God himself; even they have no alternative answer.
rows.anchor: وحيث كانوا يتلعثمون أحيانا في الجواب مخافة الإلزام قيل له عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternatives are one of the two camps: the monotheists, worshipping the sole provider with inherent power, or the idolaters, themselves powerless and sunk to the lowest contingent state; one camp must be guided and the other clearly astray.
rows.anchor: أي وإن أحد الفريقين منا معشر الموحدين المتوحد بالرزق والقدرة الذاتية العابدية وحده عزوجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is impartial language: every hearer, ally or opponent, feels fairly addressed; after the preceding proof the audience can infer which side is guided, while indirectness wins the argument more eloquently and with little contention.
rows.anchor: وهذا من الكلام المنصف الذي كل من سمعه من موال أو مناف قال لمن خوطب به : قد أنصفك صاحبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing resembles saying, God knows which of us is truthful and which is lying, leaving the listener to draw the conclusion.
rows.anchor: ونحوه قول الرجل لصاحبه قد علم الله تعالى الصادق مني ومنك وإن أحدنا لكاذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi cites Hassan's address to Abu Sufyan before his conversion: Do you revile him when you are no match for him? Your worst is ransom for your best; the verse illustrates indirect argument through a fair-sounding alternative.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول حسان يخاطب أبا سفيان بن حرب وكان قد هجا رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu al-Aswad's verse about Qushayr and Ali says that if loving Ali is good he gains it, and if it is error he still cannot be mistaken; it gives another example of indirect, tactful argument.
rows.anchor: وقول أبي الأسود : يقول الأرذلون بنو قشير طوال الدهر لا تنسى عليا بنو عم النبي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda takes aw as meaning waw, citing a line that breaking bread or breaking a bone is the same; al-Alusi considers this interpretation far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وذهب أبو عبيدة إلى أن أو بمعنى الواو كما في قوله : سيان كسر رغيفه أو كسر عظم من عظامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is a formally ordered wrap and spread: on guidance corresponds to we, and in error to you, as reason confirms, like the ordered pairing in Imru al-Qays's image of fresh and dried bird hearts.
rows.anchor: والكلام من باب اللف والنشر المرتب بأن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is not an instance of dissimulation, despite what some ignorant people claim.
rows.anchor: وأياما كان فليس هذا من باب التقية في شيء كما يزعمه بعض الجهلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent syntax needs no ellipsis: the predicate of we or you is the combined alternative, meaning one camp is characterized by one of the two states, as in saying Zayd or Amr is in the market or at home.
rows.anchor: من غير تقدير حذف إذ المعنى إن أحدنا لمتصف بأحد الأمرين كقولك زيد أو عمرو في السوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternative grammatical analyses make the phrase a predicate of inna alone with an omitted predicate for you, or a predicate of you with the predicate of we omitted as recoverable; ayyākum is a detached pronoun after inna was elided.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو خبر ( إنا ) وخبر ( إياكم ) محذوف تقديره لعلى هدى أو في ضلال مبين

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Bahr says no ellipsis is needed in this construction, though ellipsis is needed in a phrase such as Zayd or Amr is standing; al-Alusi invites reflection.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر لا حاجة إلى تقدير الحذف في مثل هذا وإنما يحتاج إليه في نحو زيد أو عمرو قائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubin is most naturally an adjective of error, but can describe both guidance and error; after aw, the adjective and pronoun remain singular.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون وصفا له ولهدى والوصف وكذا الضمير يلزم إفراده بعد المعطوف بأو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using on for guidance suggests elevation, mastery, and clear vantage, like standing high or riding a horse; using in for error depicts immersion in darkness and a cavern where one cannot find direction, a metaphor by implicit or derived image.
rows.anchor: وأدخل على على الهدى للدلالة على استعلاء صاحبه وتمكنه وإطلاعه على ما يريد

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubay's reading is إنّا أو إيّاكم أمّا على هدى أو في ضلال مبين.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة أبي ( إنا أو إياكم أما على هدى أو في ضلال مبين )
